Goal: Continue hyperparameter search on Heat2D_ComplexGeometry for MLP and PirateNets so that SDT and vanilla each have 30 trials at every K.

Plan: Keep the current Heat2D_ComplexGeometry Optuna studies and add trials until K=4 SDT and K=4 vanilla each have 30 evaluations for MLP and for PirateNets. Add vanilla trials at K=2, K=3, and K=5 until those vanilla studies also have 30 evaluations. Start a 30-trial K=1 study for each backbone with an n=3 network. Score every trial by real-GT L2RE and then refit the K-loss log-log line.
options.B:
Goal: Run SDT hyperparameter searches on PoissonND with ResNet and on PoissonND with PirateNets against the existing vanilla L2RE on each backbone.

Plan: Start one Optuna TPE study for PoissonND ResNet-SDT and one Optuna TPE study for PoissonND PirateNets-SDT. Set the search center from the best known hyperparameters on each backbone, and set the search range from the spread of earlier good trials. Enqueue those known points as the first trials, and keep the final-tune learning-rate ratio below 1. Score every trial by real-GT L2RE, and compare the new SDT best with vanilla L2RE 0.000798 on ResNet and 0.000467 on PirateNets.

options.A:
Goal: Bring Gray-Scott MLP, Gray-Scott PirateNets, and Burgers 1D ResNet staged training below the current vanilla error of each cell.

Plan: Run a staged-training hyperparameter search on each of these three cells, with 10 trials in a batch and no vanilla runs. Keep depth at 6 layers and 20000 steps. Put the first trials at the hyperparameters from the backbone of the same PDE that already beats vanilla. If a batch of 10 trials stays above vanilla, read the new best points and the search bounds, then set the next batch of 10 trials from that basin.
options.B:
Goal: Bring the Heat2D Complex Geometry staged K-loss curve to a log-log R2 of 0.98.

Plan: Expand the Heat2D Complex Geometry K=4 staged and vanilla searches from 10 trials to 30 trials. Add trials until every vanilla K has 30 evaluations. Run the missing K=1 case as a 3-layer network with 12000 steps. If the staged log-log R2 stays below 0.98, add more trials at K=4 and K=5 or try gradient clipping.

options.A:
Goal: Decide the status of Burgers1D ResNet sequential fine-tuning after the first 10-trial rescue search.

Plan: Take the 10 completed TPE trials as the rescue for Burgers1D ResNet sequential fine-tuning. Keep trial 3 as the best point, with L2RE 0.013279. Compare this value with the vanilla baseline of 0.012891. Record that sequential fine-tuning is 3.01 percent above the vanilla baseline, and leave this cell with no further hyperparameter trials.
options.B:
Goal: Decide the status of Burgers1D ResNet sequential fine-tuning after the first 10-trial rescue search.

Plan: Keep the 10 completed TPE trials and run a second 10-trial TPE batch on the same Burgers1D ResNet sequential fine-tuning cell. Place the search around the trial-3 basin. Set init_s from 0.02 to 0.8 so that init_s above 1 is out of the search. Set the learning rate from 5e-4 to 0.02, and set s12_frac, s12_lr_mult, and s3_lr_ratio around the same basin. Compare the new best L2RE with the vanilla baseline of 0.012891 after the second batch.

options.A:
Goal: Decide the next step for Burgers1D ResNet staged-depth training after three 10-trial rescue batches.

Plan: After these 30 trials, stop the Burgers1D ResNet SDT rescue on seed 0. Keep trial 18 as the best result, with L2RE 0.012963, learning rate 3.32e-3, init_s 0.055, s12_lr_mult 0.837, and s3_lr_ratio 0.460. Record the gap to vanilla L2RE 0.012891 as 0.56 percent, with ratio 1.006. Do not start a fourth 10-trial hyperparameter search for this cell.
options.B:
Goal: Decide the next step for Burgers1D ResNet staged-depth training after three 10-trial rescue batches.

Plan: Start a fourth 10-trial TPE search for Burgers1D ResNet SDT on seed 0, with 20000 steps and vanilla target L2RE 0.012891. Open a new study with learning rate from 1e-6 to 1e-3, init_s from 0.1 to 3.0, s12_frac from 0.02 to 0.25, s12_lr_mult from 5.0 to 100.0, and s3_lr_ratio from 0.1 to 0.9. Set trial 0 to the historical ITER74 values learning rate 2.44e-5, init_s 0.796, s12_frac 0.164, s12_lr_mult 28.45, and s3_lr_ratio 0.798.

options.A:
Goal: Measure Burgers1D ResNet staged depth training L2RE against the seed-0 vanilla value 0.012891.

Plan: Run a new 10-trial seed-0 search for Burgers1D ResNet staged depth training with 6 layers, width 100, and 20000 steps. Search learning rate, initialization scale, the share of steps on the first two stages, the first-two-stage learning-rate multiplier, and the fine-tune learning-rate ratio. Put the share of steps on the first two stages in the interval 0.10 to 0.25, and start trial 0 with that share equal to 0.15.
options.B:
Goal: Measure PirateNets staged depth training L2RE on Wave2D_LongTime and Heat2D_LongTime when depth grows by 2 layers per stage to 8 layers.

Plan: Run a 10-trial seed-0 search for PirateNets staged depth training on Wave2D_LongTime and a second 10-trial search on Heat2D_LongTime. Grow the network by 2 layers in each of four stages, then fine-tune all 8 layers. Use width 100 and 6000 steps in each of the five stages, and search learning rate, initialization scale, and the fine-tune learning-rate ratio.

options.A:
Goal: Fit the current support model on trampoline-only external targets while mattress files wait on official access.

Plan: Treat SLP mattress files as unavailable until the academic application is approved, and treat PmatData as a source that needs a PhysioNet login. Use the twenty digitized Park and Eager trampoline points as the external target table. Run the R5 target-domain fit on this trampoline-only table.
options.B:
Goal: Get mattress pressure targets from the SLP archive and from other public mattress data, then fit mattress and trampoline held-out targets in one table.

Plan: Search local and remote paths for the SLP zip, write download and unzip receipts, and extract any archive that can be opened. Download PmatData from PhysioNet and write mattress pressure rows with a subject-level held-out split. Add these mattress rows to the digitized Park and Eager trampoline rows, then run the R5 target-domain fit on the combined table.

options.A:
Goal: Train a small neural network that maps person and pose information to mattress pressure maps, then evaluate that network on held-out SLP subjects.

Plan: Use a trainable multilayer perceptron as the predictor head. Set decoded-map loss, learning rate, gradient clipping, and random restarts so that this network reaches decoded NRMSE of 0.05 or lower on 256 and 1024 training maps. Replay the earlier random-initialization encoded-MSE protocol on joints and metadata features. Then run the subject-held-out predictor and the content and geometry ablation with that network, and report NRMSE, contact-area error, and peak-to-mean ratio against the R20c, R22c, and R23d baselines.
options.B:
Goal: Select a pressure-map predictor head that passes a training self-anchor test, then evaluate that head on held-out SLP subjects.

Plan: Compare linear ridge and multilayer perceptron heads on decoded self-anchor using 256 and 1024 training maps. Adopt the head that reaches decoded NRMSE of 0.05 or lower, including a linear ridge head if it is the one that passes. Run a content and geometry feature ablation with that selected head, then run a subject-held-out predictor with three seeds on the same SLP split. Report held-out NRMSE, contact-area error, and peak-to-mean ratio, and compare them with the R20c, R22c, and R23d baselines.

options.A:
Goal: Set the next mattress evidence after public PmatData is confirmed to have no per-subject body shape.

Plan: Treat the missing body-shape variables as a limit on further PmatData pressure-map gains. Request extra geometry files from the PmatData authors, or keep the current posture-conditioned PmatData NRMSE of 0.572 and describe the remaining error as a lack of body-shape inputs. Leave the SLP maps on the present metadata and marker baselines.
options.B:
Goal: Test whether the PmatData physics-solver method improves pressure-map prediction on SLP.

Plan: Use the public PmatData release in its current form. Port the plate and D0 load method that already reached about 0.572 NRMSE on PmatData onto SLP pressure maps under the existing SLP subject-held-out split. Score the transferred solver with NRMSE and compare it with the current SLP metadata and body-marker results near 0.867.

options.A:
Goal: Change the SLP pressure-map evaluation from held-out-person prediction to a same-person or same-mattress protocol.

Plan: Keep scoring each predicted pressure map with pixel-to-pixel NRMSE on the recorded grid, with no search over where the person lies. Rank the plate solver, KNN, kernel ridge, and other baselines on that raw score on the current SLP subject-heldout split. Then run the next tests as same-subject few-shot adaptation, or as mattress-parameter calibration on one mattress. Keep the existing PmatData test that shifts, scales, and rotates maps as the pose-mismatch check.
options.B:
Goal: Change the SLP pressure-map evaluation from fixed-pixel NRMSE to a minimum over unknown lying pose.

Plan: Define the pressure-map error as the minimum NRMSE over translations and small rotations of the predicted map relative to the recorded map. Apply this score to the plate solver and to KNN, neural nets, ridge, and kernel ridge on the same SLP split. Choose the translation and rotation search range on training and validation maps only. Measure the same scores on SLP and PmatData at several map resolutions.

options.A:
Goal: Test whether learned pose, body-shape, and body-mass inputs, when passed through the mattress physics solver, reproduce held-out SLP pressure maps on gauge-free NRMSE.

Plan: On the SLP subject-held-out split, train models that output the inputs of the plate mattress solver, namely body pose, body shape, and body mass or an equivalent contact load. Run the solver with oracle values of those inputs and record the gauge-free NRMSE of the solver pressure maps. Train a predictor that maps BodyMAP markers to those inputs, and train an image encoder that maps raw depth, RGB, and infrared frames to those inputs. Pass each predicted input through the plate solver and score the solver pressure maps with the same gauge-free NRMSE. Compare the learned-input error with the oracle-input error on the official split, the strict-subject split, and the subject-and-posture split.
options.B:
Goal: Test whether a fine-tuned image encoder predicts SLP pressure maps with lower gauge-free NRMSE than the 72-marker kernel ridge fit.

Plan: On the SLP subject-held-out split, fine-tune ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and ViT-S so that each network maps a raw depth, RGB, or infrared frame to a pressure map. Train each backbone with encoded mean squared error, a log-space loss, and a softmax KL loss, and repeat each setting with three seeds. Score every model with gauge-free NRMSE on the same held-out rows as the BodyMAP 72-marker kernel ridge fit, whose gauge-free NRMSE is 0.817351. Count a model as a success if it is at least 0.010 lower than that kernel fit, the paired interval excludes zero, and image shuffle and label shuffle controls raise the error. Then score each success on the official split, the strict-subject split, and the subject-and-posture split.

options.A:
Goal: Get mass, load, and geometry for the solver by requesting those fields from the SLP, PmatData, and BodyMAP authors.

Plan: Rank three author requests as the next data step. Ask the SLP authors first for per-subject mass or applied load to add to the existing pressure, depth, and marker files. Ask the PmatData authors next for body geometry and mass. Ask the BodyMAP authors last for geometry, mass, and dataset splits. Run the next solver tests on the first source that returns pressure maps with geometry and with mass or load.
options.B:
Goal: Get a grid of mattress surface force values for the solver from data that is already collected.

Plan: Use the SLP height and weight labels as the scalar mass input. Set the missing field to a force value at each mattress sensor cell, measured by a load sensor that is not the pressure mat. For SLP, PmatData, and BodyMAP, label each missing field as already collected but unreleased, or never collected. Send access requests for fields labeled as already collected but unreleased. Search public mattress datasets for a published load sensor that is already paired with pressure maps.

options.A:
Goal: Test a train-only machine-learning map from PoPu Sensomatt readings to Tactilus pressure as the next validation route.

Plan: Write a protocol that treats a train-only map from the 72-cell Sensomatt grid to the 1728-cell Tactilus map as the next mattress transfer model. On the five-subject paired split, train ridge, spatial ridge, kernel ridge, an MLP decoder, and a convolutional decoder. Compare them with the train-mean map, bilinear upsample, the forward plate solver, and a linear map. If the best learned model improves gauge-free NRMSE by at least 0.020 over the linear map, or reaches 0.480 or lower, take that learned map as the PoPu validation route. Check body-part labels only as optional extra inputs.
options.B:
Goal: Test a mattress physics engine by mapping PoPu Sensomatt readings to Tactilus pressure and Tactilus pressure to Sensomatt readings.

Plan: On the five-subject paired split, score linear regression, ridge, kernel ridge, an MLP, and a CNN from Sensomatt to Tactilus, and the same model families from Tactilus to Sensomatt. Record those scores as baselines that do not use a physics engine. Fit a physical model of how mattress foam carries force between the top face and the bottom face, with parameters chosen on training subjects only, and with sample-shuffle and label-shuffle controls. Count the physics engine as successful when both directions have lower gauge-free NRMSE than the best baseline on the held-out subject.

options.A:
Goal: Produce interaction videos so a viewer can judge whether the mattress and trampoline models look physically plausible.

Plan: Render a first visual packet with the current support-model code and a 2D Pillow side view. Make at least four playable clips: a ball dropping onto a mattress, a ball dropping onto a trampoline, a block or capsule on a mattress, and one off-center or dual-contact scene. Each clip must last at least three seconds and show some surface motion. Search for Unitree G1 and SONIC or MaskedMimic assets. If a real asset is found, render a short lying or sitting rise attempt. If no asset is found, render a labeled kinematic proxy and write a missing-asset receipt. Deliver the clips for visual inspection.
options.B:
Goal: Produce interaction videos so a viewer can judge whether the mattress and trampoline models look physically plausible.

Plan: Search for a loadable Unitree G1 model. If none is found, build an articulated G1-like body. Render 3D perspective videos of four scenes: a ball on a mattress, a ball on a trampoline, a Unitree body on a mattress, and a Unitree body on a trampoline. Use a camera, lighting, and a deforming surface mesh so sag and contact are visible. For a 4 kg ball on the mattress, set the peak deflection to 30 to 80 mm, and show trampoline sag and rebound. Each clip must last at least four seconds. Deliver these four clips for visual inspection.

options.A:
Goal: Pause the mattress-data solver work and make videos of objects interacting with a mattress and a trampoline so a human can judge whether the physics looks real.

Plan: Leave PoPu, SLP, and Pmat solver fitting paused. Make four 3D clips that pair a falling ball and a Unitree G1-like humanoid with a mattress and a trampoline. Drive the scenes in MuJoCo with a perspective camera, lighting, and a surface mesh that deforms under contact. For a 4 kg ball on the mattress, set the support so peak deflection is about 30 to 80 mm, and let the trampoline show sag and rebound. Look for a real G1 or BFM model first. If none is found, use a loadable G1-like articulated body for the two humanoid clips. Do not train a policy.
options.B:
Goal: Pause the mattress-data solver work and make videos of objects interacting with a mattress and a trampoline so a human can judge whether the physics looks real.

Plan: Leave PoPu, SLP, and Pmat solver fitting paused. Make at least four 2D or 2.5D clips with the current support models and a drawing renderer: a ball on a mattress, a ball on a trampoline, a block or capsule on a mattress, and one off-center or dual-contact mattress scene. Run each clip for a few seconds at about 24 frames per second with some surface motion. After that packet, look for a Unitree G1, SONIC, or MaskedMimic model and render a humanoid clip if the model loads. If the model is missing, write a missing-asset note and a labeled proxy. Do not train a policy.

options.A:
Goal: Continue the official G1 checkpoint get-up evaluation on rigid ground, mattress, and trampoline after both published checkpoints failed the 0.05 rad joint-limit gate.

Plan: Change the joint-limit gate from 0.05 rad to 0.10 rad. Rescore the existing SONIC and ProtoMotions rigid rollouts under this gate and keep a table at 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20 rad. Rebuild the SONIC low-latency binary and test it on the rigid scene. For ProtoMotions, run each start pose that passes the 0.10 rad rigid gate on the mattress and on the trampoline with the same checkpoint and the same initial state, then compare get-up success on matched poses with a paired exact test.
options.B:
Goal: Continue the official G1 checkpoint get-up evaluation on rigid ground, mattress, and trampoline after both published checkpoints failed the 0.05 rad joint-limit gate.

Plan: Compare the project's G1 MJCF joint ranges, limit margins, contact parameters, and timestep with the IsaacGym training setup used by SONIC and ProtoMotions. Record which joints and which limit convention differ. Change those simulator settings until joint positions stay inside the MJCF ranges on rigid ground. Then run the same official checkpoint from lying and sitting starts on the mattress and on the trampoline, and inspect the videos for sinking, bounce, floating, penetration, and active get-up motion.

options.A:
Goal: Obtain a rigid get-up baseline for the official frozen Unitree G1 checkpoints by changing the joint-limit gate, then compare those checkpoints on mattress and trampoline supports.

Plan: Set the joint-limit violation gate to 0.10 rad and write that number into the evaluation protocol. Re-score the existing official SONIC and ProtoMotions rigid rollouts at 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20 rad. Keep the start poses that pass at 0.10 rad. On those poses, run the official ProtoMotions checkpoint with the same reference and initial state on rigid, mattress, and trampoline supports. Compare per-pose get-up success between the rigid support and each soft support with a paired success test.
options.B:
Goal: Obtain a rigid get-up baseline for the official frozen Unitree G1 checkpoints by editing the simulated joint ranges to the training numbers, then compare those checkpoints on mattress and trampoline supports.

Plan: Compare each joint range in the project MuJoCo G1 model with the joint-limit numbers used to train ProtoMotions and SONIC. Record differences in range, limit convention, contact parameters, and time step, including the violation that is already present when a reference pose is loaded. Change the model or contact settings that differ from the training setup. Re-run the official ProtoMotions checkpoint on the rigid scene and record the joint-limit violation. Then run the same frozen checkpoint on the mattress and trampoline and render get-up videos for visual inspection of sinking, rebound, floating, and penetration.

options.A:
Goal: Choose how to use the R80 formal paired results after the joint-limit amplification hypothesis is not supported.

Plan: Treat the R80 matrix as an evaluation of published BFM models on mattress and trampoline, and take one of three paths. The first path is to accept the eight pairs that passed the hard-floor joint-limit check, together with the mattress and trampoline-by-side observations, and start writing the paper. The second path is to collect more poses that pass the hard-floor joint-limit check and rerun the paired success-rate and joint-limit test, and the third path is to change the research question to the trampoline-by-side case where all three side poses failed.
options.B:
Goal: Check the mattress simulation by running a published BFM from lying or sitting to standing on the mattress and reviewing the rendered video of that motion.

Plan: Take a published BFM model and run the Unitree G1 from a lying or sitting pose to standing on the mattress, then render a 3D video of the full motion. Look at mattress indentation under the robot, rebound after load, and contact without floating or penetration. If a joint goes past its mechanical range during a motion that this BFM completes in its original training setup, compare the simulator joint ranges, contact parameters, and time step with that training setup, repair the mismatch, and render the video again.

options.A:
Goal: Make the mattress look softer under the robot by lowering the stiffness of the one-joint support.

Plan: Use published foam indentation numbers for a very soft mattress to choose a lower stiffness for the present single-body vertical joint. Sweep stiffness until the robot sinks about 90 mm at rest, and set damping so a small rebound is visible. Re-render the same five get-up videos and check that the sink and rebound can be seen.
options.B:
Goal: Make the mattress form a local dent under the robot while the edges stay nearly still.

Plan: Replace the single-body mattress with a grid of bodies that each have their own vertical spring, and add coupling springs between neighboring cells. Run the same five get-up poses on this grid. Re-render the five videos and check that the contact cells sink while cells far from the load stay nearly still.

options.A:
Goal: Measure the trampoline deflection-versus-radius curve under a center iron ball and rebuild the trampoline as a circular Dirichlet membrane if that curve is not a cone.

Plan: Place a 10 kg iron ball of radius 5 cm at the trampoline center and at the mattress center. After static equilibrium, record deflection versus radial distance r, fit a linear cone and an exponential cup to each profile, and require the trampoline rim displacement to be zero. If the trampoline profile is exponential, replace the 16 by 12 vertical-spring grid with a circular tension membrane that has Dirichlet edge conditions. Then render a ball-on-trampoline video and a G1-plus-BFM get-up video on that membrane.
options.B:
Goal: Expand the cupping-failure evidence by adding a second BFM checkpoint and a mattress stiffness-coupling sweep.

Plan: Repair the SONIC observation registry that previously reached only 17 of 135 tasks. If SONIC passes a rigid joint-limit gate, test it on the 380-segment cupping mattress. Download the full BFM-Zero weights, implement the backward map to a get-up latent vector z, and run the same rigid gate and cupping mattress test. Also sweep mattress total stiffness from 2000 to 6000 N/m and coupling ratio from 0.05 to 0.30 on a 3 by 3 grid with five development poses per cell. If a new checkpoint passes the rigid gate, compare it with ProtoMotions on the same five development poses.

options.A:
Goal: Make the next trampoline get-up video on a circular tensioned membrane.

Plan: Build the trampoline as a circular sheet and hold the rim at zero displacement. Carry load through in-plane tension between neighboring nodes. Place a ball at the center and record how deflection changes with radius. Take the membrane as ready for video when that profile falls in a straight line to zero at the rim and forms a cone. Then render a ball-on-trampoline video and a ProtoMotions get-up video on the same five poses.
options.B:
Goal: Make the next trampoline get-up video on a rectangular multi-segment spring grid.

Plan: Call the existing multi-segment support XML with the surface set to trampoline. Use a rectangular 16 by 12 grid of independent vertical springs and set the neighbor coupling ratio to 0.75. Keep the existing trampoline stiffness and damping totals. Run the ProtoMotions checkpoint on the same five poses. Take the run as done when the grid shows a local dent, the far field stays below 80 mm, and a get-up video is written.

options.A:
Goal: Grow evidence that a local dent in the mattress stops get-up more than the trampoline sheet.

Plan: Keep mattress get-up success of 0 out of 15 and trampoline get-up success of 3 out of 5 as the main contrast. Collect more mattress poses on the same dented mattress. Collect more trampoline poses for a larger paired sample of rigid floor and trampoline sheet. Build a new support whose sag pattern sits between a local dent and a full sheet.
options.B:
Goal: Measure how get-up success changes with hardness on the mattress and on the trampoline.

Plan: Keep the current mattress grid and the current trampoline sheet. Scale mattress spring stiffness and trampoline sheet tension across several hardness levels. At each level, average get-up success over the same poses. Plot hardness versus that mean success for the mattress and for the trampoline. On both plots, set hardness to how far a ball of fixed mass sinks when it sits still.

options.A:
Goal: Find the mattress spring count at which local depression fades and stand-up success returns.

Plan: Keep the current per-spring stiffness rule and the six stiffness multipliers. Reduce the mattress grid from 380 springs to 40, then 4, then 1. At each grid, drop the 10 kg ball and run the same five ProtoMotions stand-up poses. Record the spring count where ball sink leaves the 212 to 222 mm band and stand-up success leaves 0 out of 5, and compare that transition with the trampoline at the same spring count.
options.B:
Goal: Find the mattress stiffness assignment from a ball-sink estimate, then measure stand-up success versus hardness.

Plan: Keep the 20 by 19 spring grid from a US Bonnell queen specification. Estimate how many springs sit under the 10 kg ball from spring density times ball area, then divide ball weight by that parallel stiffness. Change how stiffness is assigned to each spring and how the 220 mm travel stop is applied. Drop the 10 kg ball and run the same five ProtoMotions stand-up poses on that grid across the hardness levels.

options.A:
Goal: Collect a mattress hardness-sinking figure that shows simulated and analytical steel-ball depths together.

Plan: Place a steel ball on the production 20 by 19 mattress at the listed hardness levels. For each level, record the simulated sinking depth and the analytical sinking depth from the spring-density estimate, and plot both curves on the same figure. Keep the coil count and bed size fixed. If the two curves disagree, update the production mattress scene and run the ball tests again. Continue the trampoline dt-convergence sweep after this mattress static check, with at most three time-step halvings per beta.
options.B:
Goal: Collect trampoline dt-convergence results for all six beta values with a cap on time-step halvings.

Plan: Keep the running trampoline characteristic-time job as the next experiment. At each beta, start from the coarse time step and allow at most three halvings of the time step. If the two time-step outcomes still disagree, record that beta as not time-step converged at the finest finished step and move to the next beta. Reuse the four completed caches at beta 0.25 and do not start a fifth finer level. Use the collected mattress oracle, mapping repair, and six-level hardness sweep as the current mattress results while this trampoline sweep finishes.

options.A:
Goal: Measure whether the compiled mattress matches the analytical sink under known loads.

Plan: Take a mattress-only physics check as the next experiment. Keep the 20 by 19 grid and the area-normalized stiffness values from the unit contract. Apply known loads in a single-cell scene, a platen scene, and a steel-ball scene. Compare compiled sink and force with the analytical values, and inspect the steel-ball sink by visual check. Make the overall pass result fail when compiled sink disagrees with the analytical sink by more than the static error limit.
options.B:
Goal: Measure how trampoline characteristic time and stable time step change with membrane tension.

Plan: Take the circular membrane as the next experiment. For each remaining tension level, compute the discrete spectrum and the characteristic time, write the time-step plan from that spectrum, and then run the same five poses at those time steps. Allow at most four time-step levels per tension. If two adjacent levels do not agree, keep the finest completed level and mark that tension as not converged. Keep the Dirichlet boundary, the five poses, and the success gates unchanged.

options.A:
Goal: Bound runner memory with process RSS checks, and collect mattress and trampoline videos.

Plan: Run the next experiment on a streaming runner that stores only online summaries and a short event window. Put each pose in a child process, and measure RSS as a function of physics step count. Record parent RSS, child RSS, and retained allocation, and compare task and physics labels with the per-step tracer. Use hundreds of gigabytes to a few terabytes of server memory, and stop a run if the memory growth rate would exhaust the host. Render 3D videos of a steel ball and an active G1 BFM on the mattress and on the circular trampoline.
options.B:
Goal: Bound runner memory with a 16 GiB cgroup cap, and collect mattress and trampoline videos.

Plan: Run the next experiment on a streaming runner that stores only online summaries and a short event window. Put each pose in a child process, and require a cgroup memory limit of 16 GiB. Record cgroup current memory, peak memory, and OOM events, and compare task and physics labels with the per-step tracer. If the node has no such cgroup, stop and ask an administrator to create a 16 GiB memory group. After that memory experiment passes, render 3D videos of a steel ball and an active G1 BFM on the mattress and on the circular trampoline.

options.A:
Goal: Test whether a streaming physics runner stays inside a 16 GiB cgroup memory limit, then collect mattress BFM videos.

Plan: At the full physics rate, keep only running statistics for force, energy, contact, and warnings. Save trajectories at 50 Hz, and keep a short window around each event. Run each pose in a child process inside a cgroup with MemoryMax set to 16 GiB. Record cgroup memory.current, memory.peak, and memory.events as the memory evidence on a fixed horizon at three dt values and on 20 episodes. Start the formal server job only if that 16 GiB cgroup is present. After those receipts pass, collect the mattress BFM videos in the paired rerun.
options.B:
Goal: Test whether a streaming physics runner keeps RSS from scaling with physics step count, then collect mattress and trampoline videos.

Plan: At the full physics rate, keep only running statistics for force, energy, contact, and warnings. Save trajectories at 50 Hz, and keep a short window around each event. Run each measurement in a child process that exits when the measurement ends. On the server, record retained bytes, parent and child RSS, and RSS slope on a short dt grid and on 20 exiting episodes. Stop the job if the early slope would consume the remaining host memory. Then render 3D videos of a ball drop and an active G1 BFM get-up on the mattress and on the circular trampoline.

options.A:
Goal: Close the main claim that local mattress sinking lowers get-up success, using the current 18-pose pair result, and send this version for paper review.

Plan: On the current mattress pair run at the nominal hardness, all 18 paired poses get up on the rigid control, all 18 fail on the soft mattress, the paired test gives p=3.8e-6, and 11 of 18 fail only when local sinking is allowed. Report the 15 physics-valid pairs as a second number. Run no new trials this round. Submit the current evidence package for review with a paper outline of the rigid-to-soft transfer gap, the 20 by 19 mattress, the circular membrane, the paired experiment, and the mechanism split.
options.B:
Goal: Make the two ProtoMotions plots of get-up success versus hardness, one for the mattress and one for the trampoline.

Plan: Use the current 18-pose mattress set and its six hardness levels. Plot mean get-up success against hardness on the mattress, averaging over those poses, and draw the rigid, soft, and mechanism arms on the same axes. Run the same official ProtoMotions get-up protocol on the circular trampoline over the same hardness grid and the same poses. Plot mean get-up success against hardness for the trampoline, and deliver these two figures as the next result.

options.A:
Goal: Measure get-up success against support hardness on the mattress and on the trampoline with the ProtoMotions policy.

Plan: Make a mattress plot and a trampoline plot. Put hardness on the x-axis and mean get-up success over the pose set on the y-axis. For the mattress, use the six hardness multipliers from the 19-pose rigid and soft trials. For the trampoline, run the official ProtoMotions policy on the same pose set at six hardness levels and plot the same way. Keep the 20 by 19 mattress grid and the ProtoMotions policy unchanged.
options.B:
Goal: Measure get-up success on four mattress arms that share one start, and repeat the same design with a second official policy.

Plan: Run the 19-pose set from one shared settling start. Use four mattress arms: a rigid copy of the same grid, a grid whose cells share one vertical motion, a grid whose cells move independently, and the standard 20 by 19 mattress. Repeat those four arms with an official HumanUP G1 policy. Compare mean get-up success across the four arms for each policy. Keep physics-invalid trials out of the success count.

options.A:
Goal: Produce the mattress figure and the trampoline figure of standup success versus support hardness.

Plan: For the mattress, plot pose-averaged standup success against hardness from the existing six-level ProtoMotions trials after excluding invalid trials. Draw the rigid-floor success as one point at infinite hardness, and add harder finite hardness multipliers so the plotted range includes both low success and near-rigid success. Pass each new hardness multiplier through the steel-ball theory and simulation check before the robot trials. For the trampoline, run pose-averaged standup trials across hardness levels with one fixed time step and plot success against hardness.
options.B:
Goal: Qualify two policy families on independent recovery recordings and measure a matched rigid-to-soft standup effect.

Plan: Scan the 403 BONES recordings for ProtoMotions until 30 recordings pass both the author's rigid-floor standup test and the project's rigid-floor standup test on five matched repeats. Find more licensed OpenTrack-compatible recovery recordings and run the same rigid qualification for OpenTrack. Then, on each qualified set, run a matched comparison of a rigid mattress, a mattress that bends as a whole, a mattress with local cupping, and a fully soft mattress, with five new repeats per recording. Set the hardness multiplier to 1 for all of these robot trials.

options.A:
Goal: Produce mattress and trampoline plots of get-up success against support hardness.

Plan: Use the ProtoMotions get-up policy on both supports. Score success on a hardness grid that shows the drop from the rigid limit to a low success rate. Plot the soft-support curve and one rigid point at infinite hardness, to the right of the stiffest finite hardness and joined by a dashed line. Reuse the six existing mattress hardness levels, add stiffer mattress levels until that drop appears, and run the same grid on the trampoline. Check each new hardness with the steel-ball theory-versus-simulation test before the get-up trials.
options.B:
Goal: Complete rigid qualification of independent get-up recordings and then compare two policy families on soft versus rigid supports.

Plan: Continue testing the remaining BONES recovery recordings on the author recovery test and on the project's rigid get-up test until all 403 recordings are scored. Count a recording as qualified only if it passes both tests. Next, qualify an OpenTrack policy family from its own motion pool with the same rigid tests. Then, on each family that has at least 30 qualified recordings, run a matched rigid versus soft get-up comparison with five repeats per recording.

options.A:
Goal: Produce a mattress hardness versus get-up success figure.

Plan: Apply the R98a validity filter to the R96b trials at alpha 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, and 8. Plot three series against alpha: full-soft mattress, common-mode mechanism, and rigid. Draw rigid as a baseline curve through those six alpha values. Draw the common-mode arm at each of the six alpha values.
options.B:
Goal: Produce a mattress hardness versus get-up success figure.

Plan: Plot the full-soft mattress success rate against alpha. Run rigid once and draw it as one point at alpha infinity to the right of the largest finite alpha, joined by a dashed line. Choose finite alpha values from near this rigid limit down to a softer regime where get-up success is low.

options.A:
Goal: Make a mattress hardness versus stand-up success figure that shows success falling from the rigid limit to a low rate.

Plan: Keep the running rigid-qualification job on its own line. Draw stand-up success against hardness for the soft mattress, and place the rigid result once as a single point at infinite hardness joined to the last finite point by a dashed line. Then add harder finite mattress values, each first checked with a steel-ball sink test against theory, until that success rate approaches the rigid point.
options.B:
Goal: Qualify at least 30 rigid stand-up clips from at least 15 source recordings on the BONES set.

Plan: Continue the running 20-clip check of the placement and contact repair until most clips pass the original rigid gates in both test environments. Then re-run all 402 clips with the same gates and the same ProtoMotions controller. Count a clip only when it completes a clean stand-up on rigid ground. End this line when the 30-clip and 15-source counts are met.

options.A:
Goal: Produce a mattress hardness-versus-get-up-success figure from matched trials at finite alpha and at rigid infinity.

Plan: Use one list of pose and repeat IDs at every finite alpha and at one rigid condition. Run those trials with the same initialization at each hardness. If a trial fails a physics or measurement check, run that same ID again until it gives a valid get-up result. Make the figure after every hardness has that same number of valid results. Choose finite alpha values so get-up success falls from the rigid limit to a low value as the mattress becomes softer. Plot only the full-soft finite-alpha curve and the single rigid infinity point.
options.B:
Goal: Produce a mattress hardness-versus-get-up-success figure from the existing six finite-alpha paired trials and a later higher-alpha extension.

Plan: Redraw the current full-soft trials at alpha 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, and 8 on the main panel. Place rigid as one point at alpha infinity to the right of alpha 8 and join it with a dashed line. Add a second panel that shows how many of the 19 poses pass the physics checks at each alpha. Compute each success rate on the poses that pass at that alpha. Then run higher alpha values on the same 19-pose set and again compute success on the poses that pass the physics checks at each new hardness.

options.A:
Goal: Obtain the mattress hardness-success curve on the final clip cohort with 50 Hz control and 6400 Hz physics.

Plan: Use the current production mattress path with a 50 Hz policy and a physics step of 0.00015625 s, with 128 physics substeps in each 0.02 s control interval. Take the final independent clip cohort from the running 402-clip requalification. Run a matched full-soft and rigid hardness-success confirmation on that cohort with the same 20 by 19 topology, official policy, success metric, and physics step. Report the finite alpha curve and one rigid limit point from this runner.
options.B:
Goal: Obtain a mattress production path with 50 Hz control, 200 Hz physics, and at least 10 times realtime on one GPU.

Plan: Use a candidate mattress path with a 50 Hz policy and a physics step of 0.005 s, with one state update in each physics step. Replay the compiled 20 by 19 law, the steel-ball theory and simulation gates, and the existing dynamic task checks at this rate. Run many environments on one GPU and measure aggregate realtime as total simulated seconds divided by one-card wall time, including reset, policy, physics, and transfers. Report the physics-check outcome and the one-GPU realtime factor for this path.

options.A:
Goal: Complete the first stage by running the same physical probes on mattress and trampoline for all three simulation routes, then fitting those probes to real measurements.

Plan: Build mattress and trampoline scenes for the Isaac PhysX FEM route, the task-specialized dynamics route, and the GPU deformable solver. Run one static and dynamic probe with the same geometry, loads, drop height, and output fields on each route for both supports. Fit the probe outputs to real mattress and trampoline measurements and score the cases that were not used in the fit. Make a cross-route table of the same observables and repair differences until the three routes match on those probes. Keep new policy families and RL paused until this probe path is done.
options.B:
Goal: Complete the first stage by getting each of the three simulation routes to produce one hardness-success plot that a person accepts, with the three plots in agreement.

Plan: For each route, finish the mattress and trampoline simulation and run one fixed existing get-up policy to make one hardness-success plot. Send each plot for human review. The first stage is complete when all three plots pass review and agree with one another. Use physical probes and real mattress and trampoline measurements to find and repair cases where a plot is unphysical or the three plots disagree. Do not start RL or a wide policy survey before the three plots exist.

options.A:
Goal: Produce Route A and Route C videos of a robot on the mattress and on the trampoline from solver states that pass the current validity gates.

Plan: Start the Route A and Route C active G1 visual inspection runs only after each matching mattress or trampoline case has a valid physics measurement. Render no Route A or Route C robot video until those gates pass. Then render the same G1 pose on the mattress and on the trampoline. Treat those four videos as the human-acceptance visual record. Record contact and penetration from the valid physics runs that feed those videos.
options.B:
Goal: Produce Route A and Route C videos of a robot on the mattress and on the trampoline from the solver states that exist now.

Plan: Render the current Route A and Route C solver states with the same active G1 pose on the mattress and on the trampoline. Mark each of the four videos as physically invalid. Count those four videos as progress records. Start the human-acceptance visual inspection only after the matching mattress or trampoline case has a valid physics measurement. Save contact and penetration receipts from the same solver state that the video shows.

options.A:
Goal: Collect the Route-C mattress decomposition and trampoline static-isolation measurements under the listed input hashes.

Plan: Move R132d to a host that has 120 GB of free disk and keep the 120 GB launch number. Copy the same code commit, the nine listed input hashes, and the same config to that host. Run the mattress decomposition cells and the trampoline static solves there, and store the residuals.
options.B:
Goal: Collect the Route-C mattress decomposition and trampoline static-isolation measurements under the listed input hashes.

Plan: Start R132d on compute node B with the Warp runtime and the nine listed input hashes that are on that host. Clear unused files so that free disk covers the run's declared output size of about 1 GB. Run the mattress decomposition cells and the trampoline static solves there, and store the residuals.

options.A:
Goal: Send Route C robot videos of the mattress and the trampoline now, and leave Route A videos until a damping check finishes.

Plan: Record one Route C video on the mattress and one Route C video on the trampoline. Send each video when it passes its own visual gate. Leave Route A videos until a damping check on Route A finishes. Continue steel-ball matching across masses and heights as a separate line.
options.B:
Goal: Match steel-ball drop behavior across Routes A, B, and C, and send Route A and Route C robot videos together when both are ready.

Plan: Find parameters so that Routes A, B, and C match steel-ball drops at two or more masses and heights on the mattress and the trampoline. Run a Route A damping check and remaining visual checks during this matching work. Send Route A and Route C videos as one set after both routes are ready.

options.A:
Goal: Get first-seed results for two remaining tasks on PySR, full FEX, LLM-SR, and Direct.

Plan: Run C3g from the cp3 family and I.29.16_0_0 from the LSR-Transform family. On these two tasks, run PySR at niterations 82 and 160, full FEX at the public scale of 1000 controller updates with 10 trees and top-10 refinement, and LLM-SR and Direct at 40 responses each. Keep the project API total at 100 dollars. Use the official splits from the remaining-nine protocol packages for these two tasks. After the two-task first-seed rows exist, use the wall time, unit cost, and recovery numbers from this round to plan the remaining seven tasks.
options.B:
Goal: Get first-seed results for the remaining nine tasks on PySR, full FEX, LLM-SR, and Direct.

Plan: Use the official splits from the remaining-nine protocol packages. Run PySR at niterations 82 and 160 on all nine tasks. Run full FEX at the public scale of 1000 controller updates with 10 trees and top-10 refinement on all nine tasks. If the project API cap is raised from 50 dollars to about 270 dollars, run LLM-SR and Direct at 40 responses on each of the nine tasks. If the cap stays at 50 dollars, run the PySR and FEX cells this round and do not run the LLM cells. After the nine-task first-seed rows exist, start repeated draws on the 13-task matrix.

options.A:
Goal: Run the four control methods on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal and record a score for each method.

Plan: Run 5-seed trials of direct LLM sampling, official LLM-SR, PySR pair search, and FEX on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal. Connect the FEX control to the original FEX source code. Write a receipt for each method that includes the seed list, the LLM-call count, the candidate count, and the wall time.
options.B:
Goal: Recover the metal_nonmetal SR-System score and compare SR-System with PySR and FEX on both tasks.

Plan: Search the SR-System artifact directory and the old metal-nonmetal branch for a recorded metal_nonmetal run. If none is found, copy the metal_nonmetal problem package into an SR-System workspace and run LLM-MCTS to produce a LOOCV accuracy. Compare SR-System with PySR and FEX at equal candidate budgets on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal.

options.A:
Goal: Measure the four baselines on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal with five seeds for each method.

Plan: Run direct LLM best-of-N, official LLM-SR, PySR pair search, and FEX tuple search as the four baselines. Make the next main experiment a five-seed score table of these methods on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal. Use ten LLM calls per seed for the LLM methods and a candidate ladder for the symbolic methods. Report the LLM methods by call count, and report PySR and FEX by search iterations, descriptor tuples, and wall time. Write the two-task table from the local receipts.
options.B:
Goal: Recover a metal_nonmetal SR-System reference and compare SR-System with the four baselines on zb_rs.

Plan: Search for a canonical SR-System metal_nonmetal run, and if none is found, copy the frozen metal_nonmetal package and run SR-System there. Make the next main experiment a comparison of SR-System with PySR and FEX on zb_rs. Run five-seed zb_rs trials of direct LLM best-of-N, official LLM-SR, PySR, and FEX tuple search. Use ten LLM calls per seed for the LLM methods and a candidate ladder for the symbolic methods. Compare the new zb_rs scores with the SR-System zb_rs score of 0.0918.

options.A:
Goal: Measure the direct and LLM-SR controls on the two material descriptor tasks with Claude Opus as the LLM provider.

Plan: Run a one-seed direct best-of-N probe and a one-seed official LLM-SR probe with Claude Opus through Claude CLI. Use call budgets 2, 10, and 26 on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal. Write a cost receipt after the direct probe and apply a 50 USD project cap before the LLM-SR probe. Then build a control table that labels Haiku rows and Opus rows separately.
options.B:
Goal: Measure the direct and LLM-SR controls on the two material descriptor tasks with an OpenAI or DeepSeek API as the LLM provider.

Plan: Run five-seed direct best-of-N and five-seed official LLM-SR with an OpenAI or DeepSeek API. Use call budgets 26 and 90 on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal. Keep LLM-SR generated candidates separate from initial seeds and write per-seed manifests. Then build a control table from these API rows and the PySR, FEX, and SISSO rows.

options.A:
Goal: Measure direct best-of-N and official LLM-SR scores on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal with Claude Opus.

Plan: Run direct best-of-N and official LLM-SR with Claude Opus on both tasks. Use call budgets of 2, 10, and 26. Score each 2D descriptor with the copied evaluators and add the Opus scores to the control table.
options.B:
Goal: Measure direct best-of-N and official LLM-SR scores on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal with DeepSeek.

Plan: Run direct best-of-N and official LLM-SR with DeepSeek on both tasks. Use call budgets of 26 and 90. Score each 2D descriptor with the copied evaluators and add the DeepSeek scores to the control table.

options.A:
Goal: Measure 5-seed DeepSeek scores for direct best-of-N and official LLM-SR on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal at 26 calls.

Plan: Launch two LLM control runs on the frozen benchmarks. The first run is DeepSeek direct best-of-N with seeds 0 through 4 and a 26-call budget on both tasks. The second run is DeepSeek official LLM-SR with the same seeds, budget, and tasks. Call the language model through the DeepSeek API for every generation. Score every candidate with the copied evaluators, then add 5-seed means and sample standard deviations as the DeepSeek rows in the next control table.
options.B:
Goal: Measure 5-seed Claude Opus scores for direct best-of-N and official LLM-SR on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal at 26 calls.

Plan: Launch two LLM control runs on the frozen benchmarks. The first run is Claude Opus direct best-of-N with seeds 0 through 4 and a 26-call budget on both tasks. The second run is Claude Opus official LLM-SR with the same seeds, budget, and tasks. Call the language model through Claude CLI for every generation. Score every candidate with the copied evaluators, then add 5-seed means and sample standard deviations as the Claude Opus rows in the next control table.

options.A:
Goal: Measure whether PySR at 50,000 and 100,000 candidates beats SR-System on zb_rs LOOCV RMSE.

Plan: Combine the 20-seed PySR runs at 50,000 and 100,000 candidates on zb_rs. Search scalar expressions on the full zb_rs labeled set and rank descriptor pairs by LOOCV RMSE. Compute mean RMSE, a 95 percent confidence interval, and the fraction of seeds with RMSE below the SR-System reference 0.0918. Write those numbers into the control table as the PySR comparison for zb_rs.
options.B:
Goal: Measure the four baselines when candidate search and selection use training rows only.

Plan: Inspect the PySR, real FEX, direct best-of-N, and official LLM-SR wrappers to see whether search, parameter fitting, or selection uses the full labeled set before LOOCV. Record that path for each method. Then rerun all four methods so that search and selection see training rows only, and score the chosen 2D descriptors once on held-out rows. Build the control table from those held-out scores.

options.A:
Goal: Find out whether PySR on zb_rs beats the SR-System LOOCV RMSE of 0.0918 more often when the seed count and the search budget increase.

Plan: Run the PySR pair-frontier wrapper on the full zb_rs table, fit expressions on all rows, and rank descriptor pairs by LOOCV RMSE. Add seeds 5 through 19 at budget 50,000, run 20 seeds at budget 100,000, and report mean RMSE, the 95 percent confidence interval, and the fraction of seeds below 0.0918.
options.B:
Goal: Find out what PySR, real FEX, direct LLM, and official LLM-SR score on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal when search uses training rows only.

Plan: Read the four control wrappers and record whether search, parameter fitting, and candidate selection use the full label vector. Rerun PySR, real FEX, direct LLM, and official LLM-SR on zb_rs and metal_nonmetal so that search and selection use training rows only, and compute the final metric once on held-out rows for each selected 2D descriptor.

options.A:
Goal: Complete official LLM-SR zb_rs split coverage to 45 of 45 rows per budget, then send the control table to review.

Plan: Take the scored DeepSeek LLM-SR zb_rs split rows from the earlier runs and generate the missing 13 rows at the 26-call budget and the 90-call budget. Collect 45 scored held-out rows for each budget. Rebuild the leakage-valid control table with mean, median, IQR, beat-rate, and the 1.5981 RMSE outlier. Send the table to review after this coverage completion.
options.B:
Goal: Send the leakage-valid control table to review with official LLM-SR zb_rs reported at 32 of 45 scored rows per budget.

Plan: Use the 32 scored DeepSeek LLM-SR zb_rs split rows at the 26-call budget and the 90-call budget. Report the beat-rate of 0 of 32 with median, IQR, and the 1.5981 RMSE outlier. Mark the LLM-SR zb_rs rows as partial coverage. Put the direct, PySR, FEX, and LLM-SR metal rows in the evidence table and send that table to review.

options.A:
Goal: Use the existing SR-System zb_rs result at a 10 to 20 candidate budget against PySR at 5000 iterations, and measure the held-out score of the already found formula.

Plan: Keep the SR-System search at its 10 to 20 candidate budget. Set the PySR comparison at 5000 iterations. Re-score the descriptor formula that SR-System already found on zb_rs on the existing held-out splits, and record how far the score moves from 0.0918.
options.B:
Goal: Score the existing SR-System zb_rs descriptor on the held-out splits and use those scores as the SR-System numbers in the baseline table.

Plan: Take the descriptor formula that SR-System already found on zb_rs. Score that formula on the existing held-out splits that the baselines already use. Put these split scores into the baseline table as the SR-System numbers next to the baselines that already search on training compounds only.

options.A:
Goal: Get SR-System zb_rs held-out scores by running a new search on each of the 15 train splits.

Plan: For every existing zb_rs split, run SR-System on the train rows only. Choose one descriptor from that search, then score it on the matching held-out rows. Use the 15 held-out scores as the SR-System numbers in the comparison with the current split-search baseline table.
options.B:
Goal: Get SR-System zb_rs held-out scores by scoring the node 0010 descriptor on each of the 15 held-out splits.

Plan: Read the descriptor formula from node 0010 of the existing zb_rs SR-System run. Score that formula on each of the 15 held-out splits. Record the 15 held-out scores and the change from 0.0918, and use those scores in the comparison with the current split-search baseline table.

options.A:
Goal: Make a six-method score table for zb_rs and metal_nonmetal from the current split results.

Plan: Put SR-System, Direct best-of-N, official LLM-SR, PySR, real FEX, and SISSO into the table. For each method write Mean, Median, and Best and Worst from the current split scores, and add columns for protocol status and data source. On metal_nonmetal, set the Best value of Direct best-of-N, official LLM-SR, and PySR to 1.0. On zb_rs, write a refit SR-System row with Best 0.068 and Worst 0.122, and an original-coefficient SR-System row with Best 0.065 and Worst 0.122. Leave the zb_rs SISSO cell empty.
options.B:
Goal: Make a six-method score table for zb_rs and metal_nonmetal from the current split results.

Plan: Put SR-System, Direct best-of-N, official LLM-SR, PySR, real FEX, and the literature reference into the table. For each method write the mean split score as the table value. On zb_rs, write SR-System as the mean 0.0918 of the existing formula on the 15 splits, and write the literature reference formula as RMSE 0.1045. On metal_nonmetal, write the mean split accuracy of Direct best-of-N, official LLM-SR, PySR, and real FEX, and write the SISSO external formula as accuracy 0.9866. Use the columns method and mean score.

options.A:
Goal: Set the original-paper claim for the internal dimension d from the Qwen2.5 energy series.

Plan: Finish the 512-prompt energy generations on Qwen2.5. Compute dimension d on the 103-prompt series and on the 512-prompt series, and choose a claim for d from those two tables. Record chi as the output-embedding fluctuation curve that peaks near T=0.3. Run the next analysis on output-end energy curves and dimension fits.
options.B:
Goal: Test whether chi can peak at T_c, and measure criticality on internal transformer quantities.

Plan: Take the not-sharp chi curve as a question of definition or of the measured layer or quantity. On the Qwen2.5-0.5B generations, recompute chi under other definitions and on other layers. Extract QK, attention, and OV at several layers, and compute the order parameter, the temperature derivative, and chi. Compare the interior peak temperature to the output energy T_c near 1.1.

options.A:
Goal: Measure whether the chi_attn peak temperature changes as the attention window grows on Qwen3-4B simple-wiki prompts.

Plan: Extract connected chi on Qwen3-4B simple-wiki prompts at window sizes 128, 256, 512, and 1024. In this first extraction, compute each connected-chi confidence interval with 1000 bootstrap resamples for every head, temperature, and window. Then read T_peak at each window and judge whether the peak drifts with window size.
options.B:
Goal: Measure whether the chi_attn peak temperature changes as the attention window grows on Qwen3-4B simple-wiki prompts.

Plan: Extract connected chi on Qwen3-4B simple-wiki prompts at window sizes 128, 256, 512, and 1024. In this first extraction, compute each connected-chi confidence interval with 100 bootstrap resamples. Then use that first T_peak result to decide whether to raise the bootstrap count or to move to a different experiment.

options.A:
Goal: Get a finite-size scaling result for connected chi_attn on Qwen3-4B using S2 prompts.

Plan: Extract connected chi_attn with 12 prompts and 16 seeds for window sizes 128, 256, 512, and 1024. Estimate T_peak at each window size with 100 bootstrap samples. If T_peak changes by more than 0.1 across window size and the change is monotonic, repeat the measurement with 48 prompts, 64 seeds, and 1000 bootstrap samples. If T_peak does not change by more than 0.1, switch to another experiment.
options.B:
Goal: Get a finite-size scaling result for connected chi_attn on Qwen3-4B using S2 prompts.

Plan: Extract connected chi_attn with 48 prompts and 64 seeds for window sizes 128, 256, 512, and 1024. Estimate T_peak at each window size with 1000 bootstrap samples. If T_peak changes by more than 0.1 across window size and the change is monotonic, treat the result as a phase transition. If T_peak does not change by more than 0.1, treat the result as a crossover.

options.A:
Goal: Decide which layer, observable definition, RoPE setting, and corpus give a sharp temperature-criticality signal.

Plan: On Qwen3-4B, compute hidden-state energy and magnetization at the output embedding and at the first, quarter-depth, mid-depth, three-quarter-depth, and last decoder layers. At those same layers, compute connected chi, raw chi, thermal chi, and specific heat. Repeat the measurements with RoPE applied and with RoPE removed. Run the same grid on more than one corpus, including scifact and FineWeb. Rank the combinations by the location and height of the energy or susceptibility peak versus temperature.
options.B:
Goal: Decide which confidence-interval rule can recover a replicable chi_attn signal from the stored 4B and 8B attention runs.

Plan: Take the stored per-temperature chi_attn files from the Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B scifact runs. Add bootstrap resampling to the gate-calibration script. On those files, score a wider T_c window, a lower ratio threshold, a layer-pooled head score, and a point-estimate rule. Compare the token-shuffle null with the random-edge null on the same heads. Choose one rule from this search. Then score the 4B and 8B replication files under that rule.

options.A:
Goal: Determine whether including RoPE changes hidden-state layer energy on the grids where energy already shows a temperature trend.

Plan: On Qwen3-4B, reuse the existing layer-energy prompts, layers, and temperature grid from the R55 and R62 corpora. For each corpus, run the model on the same prompt sequences twice and collect hidden-state energy: one forward with RoPE on, and one forward that disables RoPE inside attention. Compute signed T_c and the energy-versus-temperature curve for both modes. Write a table of per-layer differences in T_c and in the energy curve. Check that embedding-layer energy is the same in both modes.
options.B:
Goal: Determine whether including RoPE changes the QK susceptibility result on the collected pre-RoPE and post-RoPE chi grids.

Plan: Take the R94 and R95q pre-RoPE and post-RoPE QK chi tables for the existing model scales, layers, and corpora. For each mode, record whether the chi peak sits at the lowest measured temperature, and whether the peak height is less than twice the positive median. Summarize those boundary-peak and weak-peak counts as the RoPE include-or-exclude result. Continue to report layer energy from the current standard forward pass that already uses RoPE. Write a summary table of these chi counts for the current evidence set.

options.A:
Goal: Report how the defined energy, and chi, change across layers when RoPE is on and when RoPE is off.

Plan: Read the Qwen3 4B and Qwen3 32B energy tables that list T_c at embedding, L0, L9, L18, L27, and L35 with RoPE and without RoPE. Read the matching Qwen3 4B chi tables. For each corpus, write energy T_c by layer in both settings and write whether chi still shows a peak. Use those lists to say which RoPE setting keeps T_c close across layers.
options.B:
Goal: Set the next project direction after shuffled-token null reproduced layer T_c and after the V4 finite-size scaling, Binder, and overlap checks.

Plan: Write a paper whose main claim is that the output-side temperature transition does not come from Transformer internal coupling. Use the shuffled-token null T_c match and the V4 finite-size scaling, Binder, and overlap numbers as the evidence for that claim. The other option is to define a new internal observable from the literature, write a success rule before any run, and measure that new quantity on the same models and corpora.

options.A:
Goal: Test whether text place names remain usable as spatial memory when room type, graph size, and goal type change.

Plan: Run a real vision-language model on indoor images and measure how often two views of the same place receive the same name. Then change the room type, the graph size, and the goal type. Record when two places are joined by mistake, when one place is split by mistake, and when a goal is mapped to the wrong node. Report the rooms, graph sizes, and goal types where the names remain usable.
options.B:
Goal: Test whether extra view and neighbor naming cues can support text-graph vision-language navigation.

Plan: Run a real vision-language model on indoor images and measure how often two views of the same place receive the same name. Then add naming cues that combine multiple views, use neighbor rooms to tell similar places apart, and set how specific each name is. Measure how often the same place is matched and how often two places are joined by mistake after these cues are added. Test routing on the text adjacency graph built from these names.

options.A:
Goal: Measure how well an LLM can output name-list routes on Matterport3D graphs that use VLM place names.

Plan: Use the Matterport3D connectivity graph as the map. Name each node with a Qwen2.5-VL-7B alias from the viewpoint image, and make a unique-name variant of those aliases. Give DeepSeek-R1 the named adjacency list and ask it for a route as a list of place names. Score each route by whether every consecutive pair is a real edge and by how much longer the path is than BFS. Repeat this test on at least five Matterport3D scans whose images cover at least 80 percent of viewpoints.
options.B:
Goal: Measure how well A* can navigate Matterport3D scans on a named map built by a VLM from images.

Plan: On one Matterport3D scan with at least 80 percent image coverage, use Qwen2.5-VL-7B to name each viewpoint from its image. Use the same VLM to decide which adjacent views are the same place, and build a named graph from those decisions and the connectivity edges. Run A* on this graph for random start-goal pairs, and score success rate and SPL against A* on the Matterport3D connectivity graph. Then run the same steps on at least five Matterport3D scans whose images cover at least 80 percent of viewpoints.

options.A:
Goal: Decide what to run next after the R2R vocabulary-overlap diagnostic returned a low ceiling.

Plan: Take the current R2R and R4R runs as the evidence base for a thesis decision. Put three paths in front of the user. Path one keeps the named place graph and uses visual matching at each following step. Path two runs REVERIE and SOON on the same pipeline to test object-goal instructions. Path three writes a report from the R2R vocabulary mismatch numbers, the oracle routing result, and the existing R4R score. Launch the next experiment series after the user selects one of these paths.
options.B:
Goal: Decide what to run next after the R2R vocabulary-overlap diagnostic returned a low ceiling.

Plan: Run the current named-place navigation system on R2R, R4R, RxR, REVERIE, SOON, and CVDN. Use the official or public split of each dataset and the end-to-end protocol that a paper table would report. On R2R, score object-viewpoint following on the full val-unseen split. On R4R, score the all-instruction expansion of val-unseen. On REVERIE, SOON, CVDN, and RxR, add a task conversion and produce one scored run with official labels and the task success metric. After each listed dataset has a scored result, send the package for review.

options.A:
Goal: Test whether place naming on the eight-scan visual sample can pass the recall and per-scan false-merge gate.

Plan: Use the existing 390 Qwen2.5-VL-7B place cards and the 320-pair visual sample from j33a, with each card storing a short name and anchors. Score every j35 linker rule and threshold on a gate that requires recall of at least 70 percent, aggregate false merge of at most 20 percent, and every scan false merge of at most 20 percent. On scans D7G3, Z6MF, and pLe4, assign a cause to each false merge and false negative. Re-check those pairs with GPT-4.1-mini, giving the model up to two extra neighboring MP3D images per endpoint. Run an eight-scan route evaluation only when a candidate meets the gate.
options.B:
Goal: Test whether place naming on the eight-scan visual sample can pass the recall and per-scan false-merge gate.

Plan: Use the same 390 real MP3D viewpoints and the same 320-pair visual sample from j33a. Call gpt-5.5 to write one card per viewpoint that contains a short name, stable anchors, and a detailed description of visible objects, layout, and distinctive cues. Run the linker on the 320 pairs with those cards, and report aggregate and per-scan recall and false merge. Score that linker on a gate that requires recall of at least 70 percent, aggregate false merge of at most 20 percent, and every scan false merge of at most 20 percent. Run an eight-scan route evaluation only when a candidate meets the gate.

options.A:
Goal: Test whether GPT-5.5 detailed place cards pass the naming gate on the 8-scan set after every pair is labeled with the strict room-level same-place rule.

Plan: Label the original 8-scan 320 visual pairs with the strict room-level same-place rule used on the 4 val-unseen scans. Use GPT-5.5 as the judge for this label pass. Recompute the existing GPT-5.5 linker outputs against these labels and report recall and false-merge with the four naming-gate conditions. Then write GPT-5.5 detailed cards and run the linker on more val-unseen Matterport scans under that same rule until the same-place count is at least 64.
options.B:
Goal: Test whether a local 32B or 72B vision-language model can write place cards that pass the 8-scan naming gate.

Plan: Serve a 32B or 72B open-source vision-language model on the server GPUs. Write detailed place cards for the 390 viewpoints in the current 8-scan Matterport set, using the same card prompt as the GPT-5.5 runs. Run the linker on the 320 visual pairs at threshold 0.25 and record recall and false-merge under the current same-place labels. If the four naming-gate conditions pass and recall is within 10 points of 72.33 percent, use this local model to write cards for later naming runs.

options.A:
Goal: Resume GPT-5.5 route-list stress on the eight real named graphs and independent GT repair on the 53 disputed pairs.

Plan: When the OpenAI account accepts jobs, run GPT-5.5 on 14 of the 1392 prepared dense route queries on the eight real named graphs with the existing j39d script, then on 139 queries, then on all 1392 queries, and record the expected dollar cost before each of those three stages. In the same round, run GPT-5.5 on all 53 disputed visual pairs under the strict room-level contract, using the batch file that is already uploaded. Count this work against a 200 dollar API budget, with about 92 dollars already used.
options.B:
Goal: Resume GPT-5.5 route-list stress on the eight real named graphs and independent GT repair on the 53 disputed pairs.

Plan: When the OpenAI account accepts jobs, run GPT-5.5 on all 1392 prepared dense route queries on the eight real named graphs with the existing j39d script. In the same round, run GPT-5.5 on all 53 disputed visual pairs under the strict room-level contract, using the batch file that is already uploaded. Count this work against a 500 dollar API budget, with about 92 dollars already used.

options.A:
Goal: Collect end-to-end named-route scores on the six official VLN benchmarks.

Plan: Run the current string-route planner with route-exhaustion STOP on R2R, R4R, REVERIE, SOON, CVDN, and RxR. For each dataset, complete nested 1 percent, 10 percent, and full val-unseen splits. Use gpt-5.6-sol with reasoning-effort max for every model call. Continue each run until the selected split is complete, then start the next scale on the same pipeline. After the full split of all six datasets is collected, send the results to review.
options.B:
Goal: Collect end-to-end named-route scores on the six official VLN benchmarks.

Plan: Run the current string-route planner with route-exhaustion STOP on R2R, R4R, REVERIE, SOON, CVDN, and RxR. For each dataset, complete nested 1 percent, 3 percent, and 10 percent val-unseen splits, and reuse each finished split inside the next split. Use gpt-5.6-sol with reasoning-effort medium for every model call. Shuffle the selected episodes before each run, stop the run at 6 hours, and score the finished random prefix. After the 10 percent stage of all six datasets is collected, send the results to review.
